newsitem.title: USA: DRUG GROUP FALLS AFTER MORGAN STANLEY CUTS SECTOR.
newsitem.headline: DRUG GROUP FALLS AFTER MORGAN STANLEY CUTS SECTOR.

text.p: Shares of U.S.-based drug companies slumped Monday after Morgan Stanley reduced its recommended portfolio weighting of the drug sector based upon a recent uptick in the group's selling, general and administrative expenses.

Morgan Stanley pharmaceuticals analyst Paul Brooke said in the report he was cutting his recommendation from overweight to market weight in large part because the increased spending "takes out the opportunity for upside earnings surprise in the near term."
Warner-Lambert Co led the selloff, with its shares off 5-7/8 to 130-1/4 near midday. Merck & Co was off 3-5/8 to 95-3/16. Eli Lilly and Co slipped 3-15/16 to 108-7/8.
Schering-Plough Corp fell 2-3/8 to 49, while Pfizer Inc dropped 2-3/16 to 53-1/8. Johnson & Johnson better withstood the selloff, slumping 13/16 to 58-3/8.
The Morgan Stanley report said outperformance of the drug sector was better than expected in the first half of 1997 "in a (stock) market that was itself better than expected."

The report said the sector had also benefitted from diminished patent concerns, the inability of managed care providers to control drug usage and costs, and continuation of favorable drug approval rates by the U.S. Food and Drug Admininistration.

But Morgan expressed concern that the negative foreign exchange effect of a stronger dollar, seen in the first half of the year, would likely worsen in the second half. "It highlights the difficulties in European markets," the report said.

And, the report cautioned that first-half performance "was a honeymoon as momentum investors came into the group," adding some of the momentum buying "was not fundamentally based or understood" -- leaving the group susceptible to weaker performance.
"Morgan has caused a few clients to get out of the group. It's a pretty substantial downdraft for the day," said Mario Corso, a Rodman & Renshaw pharmaceuticals analyst.
But Corso said he remained bullish on the sector short-term and long term, adding Monday's slump was less than spectacular when compared with the group's gains this year.

He said stock appreciation for the seven biggest U.S. pharmaceuticals companies jumped 49 percent during the first seven months of 1997, compared with a 27 percent gain for companies in the S&P 500 composite index.
He predicted the drug sector would continue its winning streak despite its ongoing investment push in research and development, advertising and other areas.
Alex Zisson, a Hambrecht & Quist drug analyst, said he saw no other industry or government news that would explain Monday's decline.
"Sometimes all it takes is one analyst to spur selling. Psychology is everything, particularly when the drug group has skyrocketed even more than other industries this year," he said.
Foreign-based drugmakers showed mixed fortunes Monday, with Glaxo Wellcome Plc edging slightly higher, but SmithKline Beecham Plc falling 2-1/8 to 89-11/16 in New York.
